questions.question: How does the new alerting approach group model-serving requests by the stages they pass through to reduce noisy alerts and speed up root cause analysis?

An alert route-matrix generator then uses those cohort rollups to build a route × stage alert matrix that attributes SLO violations to the most likely pipeline stages and biases escalation to the top-k responsible stages, reducing per-route alert noise and speeding RCA.

questions.question: During a major production outage, what is the prescribed sequence of actions for the first 60 to 90 minutes, from opening the live coordination call through confirming the service is healthy again?

(2) Perform quick impact triage by confirming affected services via dashboards and classifying scope (regional/global; data/control plane), then produce a short impact statement (5-10m). (3) Stabilize traffic using graduated controls (rate limits, routing/traffic division to healthy regions) and, where available, fall back to lighter model variants or reduced sequence-length modes (10-20m). (4) Execute a hotfix window by applying validated, small, reversible mitigations from the relevant service runbooks and document all changes in the incident channel (20-40m). (5) Validate restoration by running synthetic probes and verifying p95/p99 latency and error rates are returning to baseline, capturing pre/post metrics and commands used (30-50m).

questions.question: Customers behind strict corporate proxies are seeing 4xx failures when the quickstart templates add telemetry tags. What tagging approach and opt-out setting should we use, and how will that affect TTFS and activation KPI measurement?

questions.question: How do we decide whether a streaming disconnect is a client abort or a platform-caused failure for SLO and error budget accounting, and how should that be reflected in the SLA availability calculation and the customer-facing Support response?
questions.gold_answer:
Classify streaming disconnects using gateway stream-close telemetry correlated with upstream attempt signals. Mark as client_abort only when (1) the gateway observed a client-initiated close/reset before the normal terminal event and (2) there is no coincident upstream failure (no upstream 5xx/timeout/reset) in a short correlation window (default ~2s). If there is an upstream/gateway failure signal (upstream_reset, gateway_error/idle_timeout/proxy_write_error, router_failover_midstream, etc.) or attribution is ambiguous, treat it as platform-caused and count it as a bad stream.
For SLO/error budget: client_abort/customer-cancelled disconnects are excluded from streaming reliability (and excluded from streaming/latency SLIs per the exclusion rules); platform-caused disconnects count against streaming reliability, and for streaming "availability/success" the request is only good if the stream is established and ends cleanly (terminal event + clean close).
For SLA availability (calendar month): an Eligible streaming request is failed if it ends in a Redwood-attributable stream error/disconnect (or 5xx); client aborts/customer timeouts and customer/network issues supported by edge telemetry are excluded. If disconnect cause is ambiguous, default to counting it as Redwood-attributable for SLA/SLO accounting.
Support response should mirror this: explain that not all streaming failures appear as a single 5xx because the stream is already open; we use terminal stream events to classify completed vs error vs client-abort. Ask for x-redwood-request-id(s), timestamps (UTC), region, client error text, whether a terminal SSE event was received, and client/proxy timeout settings; share mitigations like increasing proxy idle/read timeouts, bounding max_tokens/response duration, and ensuring the client continuously reads the stream.

questions.question: For an enterprise ticket like SUP-1842 where streaming disconnects happen in us-east, when should we escalate from a Support bridge to a formal incident and post a status page update, and what customer update cadence and credits wording should we use?
questions.gold_answer:
Escalate from a Support bridge to a formal incident (#incidents) and open a status page incident when the issue is no longer customer-specific triage and meets any of the comms-alignment criteria (default to YES unless explicitly waived by IC + CS leadership). Concretely, move to #incidents and treat as incident-worthy if any are true: (1) suspected or confirmed multi-customer impact (2+ customers with the same symptom in the same region/model within 60 minutes, or duplicate inbound volume), (2) evidence or strong suspicion of regional/service degradation even if only one enterprise customer reported first, based on telemetry such as streaming resets/truncations >= 0.5% of streams for 10 minutes, 5xx >= 2% for 10 minutes, timeouts >= 1% for 10 minutes, or p95 latency >= 2x baseline for 15 minutes (do not wait for perfect metrics if impact is credible), (3) mitigation requires coordinated on-call action that changes production behavior (rollback, traffic shift, routing/fallback changes, capacity moves) or you need cross-team coordination/comms roles, (4) tier-critical impact (Enterprise/Dedicated/Private) where SLA or credits concerns are expected, or (5) impact persists beyond ~15 minutes without quick mitigation (if uncertain, open a cautious "Investigating" status incident). Once in #incidents, keep the Support bridge only for customer-specific coordination and mirror the IC as the source of truth.

Customer update cadence for Enterprise: if P0, first response within 15 minutes (24/7) and meaningful updates every 30 minutes while active; if P1, first response within 30 minutes (24/7) and updates every 60 minutes while actively mitigating. For any declared incident, mirror the IC/comms lead cadence and always include the next update time; if you are blocked or there is no change, still send a time-based "still investigating/monitoring, next update at X" update.

Credits wording: do not promise credits and do not write "SLA breach" or any admission of fault. Use: "If youd like to request service credits per your agreement, were reviewing the incident timeline and observed impact against the applicable SLA terms and can confirm any applicable credits once the impact assessment is finalized." For SUP-1842 specifically, if pressed, commit only to a decision timeline: "Well get back to you by Wednesday, Feb 11." Any goodwill credit or credit amount requires CS leadership approval (Jasmine Liu; coordinate via Rachel Kim) and route any contract interpretation to Legal (Sofia Mendes); default credit application is a billing adjustment on the next invoice unless CS leadership explicitly approves mid-cycle.

questions.question: Which streaming event names and tool-call fields are we standardizing on for SDK examples and golden fixtures, and how should we map OpenAI-compat tool-call deltas into that model?
questions.gold_answer: Standardize SDK examples + golden fixtures on these canonical stream event types: response.started, message.delta, tool_call.delta, tool_call.final (aka tool_call.done), message.final, response.completed (aka response.done), plus response.error and response.interrupted. Tool-call fields are: tool_call_id (the stable identifier used everywhere, including tool results), name, arguments_delta (streamed fragment as a string), and arguments (complete JSON string on final); tool results are role="tool" with tool_call_id and content (typically JSON-stringified). For OpenAI-compat streaming, map each delta.tool_calls[i] to this model by setting tool_call_id = tool_calls[i].id, name = tool_calls[i].function.name, and arguments_delta = the new appended substring of tool_calls[i].function.arguments (or the provided fragment); accumulate per tool_call_id, and when the tool call is complete (finish_reason tool_calls / end of tool-call emission / message final), emit tool_call.final with arguments = the full accumulated arguments string, then JSON-parse/validate only at that point.

questions.question: If a Private upgrade fails on a Postgres migration lock timeout, what is the recommended operator path to recover or roll back, and what upgrade artifacts and audit events need to be captured for change management?
questions.gold_answer:
On a Private upgrade Postgres migration lock-timeout failure: stop further progression (do not proceed to data-plane changes), capture the current installer upgrade status/last state and generate a support bundle including the upgrade trace. Attempt forward recovery first by clearing the lock contention: scale down the control-plane deployments to release stale connections, inspect Postgres for long-running transactions and lock waits (pg_stat_activity / lock info), terminate the blocking backend PID (pg_terminate_backend) and retry the migration step (re-run the migration job / re-apply the control-plane stage per the installer plan). If the lock cannot be cleared quickly, migrations appear partially applied, or the plan indicates the migration stage is not safely reversible, move to rollback decisioning: use the installer rollback path only if the upgrade state shows a valid rollback entry point and migrations are marked reversible; otherwise treat rollback as blocked/unsafe and perform restore-from-backup as the authoritative fallback (scale down workloads to prevent writes, restore the control-plane DB from the pre-upgrade snapshot/dump associated with the plan, reconcile Helm releases/values/manifests to the pre-upgrade pinned versions recorded in the upgrade state, then bring CP up and verify CP health before restoring DP and running postchecks).

For change management, retain and attach: the generated upgrade plan (plan.json / upgrade-plan.json, plus a short summary), the precheck report (precheck-report.json, including any WARN acknowledgements), the backup report/manifest (backup-report.json plus backup_id and snapshot IDs or dump URIs, verification result, and encryption/KMS mode), the upgrade execution outputs (upgrade-report.json and/or persisted state dir/UpgradeRun record with upgrade_id, from/to versions, plan hash, backup_id, per-stage step results) and relevant Kubernetes job logs (migration job) plus installer logs; include rollback-report.json if rollback is attempted, or restore logs/evidence if a backup restore is performed; and the generated support bundle with upgrade trace (redacted of secrets). Audit events minimum set: upgrade_started, prechecks_passed or prechecks_failed, backup_completed or backup_failed, upgrade_completed or upgrade_failed, and if used rollback_invoked plus rollback_completed or rollback_failed (and restore_started/restore_completed for environments requiring restore audit), with environment/cluster id, operator identity, from_version/to_version, upgrade_plan_id/plan hash, upgrade_id/execution id, backup_id, and timestamps.

questions.question: In the March 2026 incident where long-lived Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams would reconnect after a brief upstream TCP reset and then show duplicated heartbeat frames while sometimes never emitting the terminal end-of-stream event, what was the root cause and what server-side fix resolved it?
questions.gold_answer: Root cause was a race in the sse-gateway after a brief upstream TCP RST where the in-flight terminal end event flush interleaved with scheduled keepalive/heartbeat work, causing duplicated heartbeat frames and sometimes dropping the terminal end-of-stream event when the client resumed quickly. The fix was PR 2147 on the server to make terminal end emission atomic and strictly ordered ahead of heartbeats, and to delay/guard resume acceptance with a short grace window so a reconnect can't interleave with the final flush.

questions.question: In the hosted API incident in late April 2026 where streaming requests started returning 502/504 and non-streaming requests also saw a sharp tail-latency increase, what was the underlying trigger (involving an edge keepalive/connection-TTL change) and what immediate mitigations were used to restore service?
questions.gold_answer: It was triggered by an edge configuration change that cut upstream connection keepalive/TTL from 90s to 10s, increasing connection churn and exposing a streaming-proxy TCP write-stall bug that caused 502/504 on streaming and sharp tail-latency for non-streaming. Service was restored by rolling restarting the streaming-proxy fleet to clear stuck buffers, rolling back the edge TTL/keepalive setting to 90s, and applying temporary traffic shaping (soft concurrency limits and rejecting new sessions on overloaded proxies).

questions.question: For Incident Bot v2, when responders use break-glass during a Sev0/Sev1 incident to view tenant-scoped config diffs or run privileged telemetry queries, which audit events must be emitted and how long are those audit events retained (SIEM vs immutable archive)? Also, what baseline vs break-glass permission scopes does the bot use for these reads?
questions.gold_answer: When break-glass is used in a Sev0/Sev1 incident, the bot must emit audit events for the break-glass session (incident_bot.break_glass.activate and incident_bot.break_glass.deactivate when it expires/is revoked) and for each privileged read: incident_bot.config_diff.read for tenant-scoped config diff reads and incident_bot.telemetry.query for privileged tenant-scoped telemetry queries (with break_glass=true and a break_glass_session_id on calls made under break-glass). These audit events are retained 400 days in the searchable SIEM and 7 years in an immutable/WORM archive. For permissions, baseline reads use config.read:diff_redacted and telemetry.read:diagnostics_templates; break-glass uses config.read:diff_expanded_redacted for expanded redacted config diffs and telemetry.read:tenant_scoped for tenant-scoped telemetry templates.

questions.question: After the Feb 22, 2026 SEV-2 where Console rollout actions caused a rollback loop, which HTTP status code was wrongly treated as retryable, what server-side idempotency change was added for rollback requests, and (per the Dedicated staged rollouts audit-log spec) which service must emit the canonical audit events and what identifiers are used to de-duplicate retries?
questions.gold_answer: It wrongly retried HTTP 409 Conflict. The fix was to require a server-side Idempotency-Key for rollback requests so retries return the same result. Per the Dedicated staged rollouts audit-log spec, the dedicated-pool-rollouts-service must emit the canonical audit events, and retries are de-duplicated using the idempotency_key (with event_id used by the audit pipeline as the unique dedupe/primary key).
